items.text: Since hydra and the immortal jellyfish do not exhibit obvious signs of aging, they are often called biologically immortal. <break time="0.8s" /> This does not mean they do not die. <break time="0.8s" /> Nor does it even mean that they cannot die of biological causes. <break time="0.8s" /> But, unlike most every animal, their likelihood of dying does not increase with age. <break time="0.8s" /> Species such as hydra and the immortal jellyfish excite gerontologists because they may provide clues about how to defeat the aging process. <break time="0.8s" /> But their property of being able to regenerate entire body parts, or even a whole organism, makes them more similar to trees than to us. <break time="0.8s" /> Although we may learn some fascinating things about their lack of apparent aging, it is not at all clear how relevant those findings will be to human aging. <break time="0.8s" /> Sometimes biology is universal, especially if it relates to fundamental mechanisms. <break time="0.8s" /> But in other cases, even discoveries in rats or mice, which are mammals and biologically much closer to us, are difficult to translate into humans. <break time="0.8s" /> It may be a very long time before any findings gained from hydra or jellyfish are useful to us.
